newsitem.title: USA: Inventory growth cushions U.S. economic slowdown.
newsitem.headline: Inventory growth cushions U.S. economic slowdown.

text.p: Fatter inventories cushioned the economy's third-quarter slowdown, the Commerce Department said Friday, holding it on a path of modest expansion that seemed set to carry into 1997.

Gross domestic product grew at a revised 2.1 percent annual rate in the quarter, less than half the 4.7 percent pace in the second quarter, but fractionally higher than the 2 percent rate estimated a month ago, the department said in its second and last report on third-quarter performance.
GDP measures total production of goods and services within a country's borders.

Analysts said the slower rate of growth in the third quarter was healthy and that while growth going forward would probably be modest, that was preferable to faster growth that could fuel a pickup in inflation.

"A very flat economy with very high employment and very low inflation -- what a deal," said William Dunkelberg, chief economist at the National Federation of Independent Business, a group representing about 500,000 small- and medium-sized businesses.

During the third quarter, businesses of all types boosted inventories by $34.5 billion instead of the $32.8 billion previously estimated, the department said. That was nearly five times the $7.1 billion inventory buildup in the second quarter and helped buoy growth in the third quarter.
But the revision did nothing to change the picture of an economy that cooled during the summer after a sizzling first half.

"Growth was markedly lower in the third quarter than in the second, and most components contributed to the slowdown except business investment in structures, equipment and inventories," the department said.

Robert Dederick, economic consultant to Northern Trust Co. in Chicago, said the third quarter was "a payback quarter" -- consumer spending slowed after a spring surge while government spending picked up after being sluggish in the second quarter.

"But it's a quarter that was eminently satisfying," he added. "Growth is in line with what the economy's long-term potential is perceived to be, inflation is well-contained and there are no significant distortions."

Early signs point to slight pickup in the current quarter -- Dederick estimated a 2.7 percent annual growth rate based on stronger consumer spending -- though no official estimate of performance will be available until a month from now.

Reports on fourth-quarter activity so far have been mixed, ranging from a pickup in home building last month to higher weekly jobless claims last week, a sign of moderating strength in the labour market.

Dunkelberg said a survey of federation members in November showed that 11 percent expected more vigorous economic growth by mid-1997 but about 21 percent saw weaker growth. On balance, expansion was expected to continue at a 2 percent to 2.5 percent rate.
That should keep interest rate changes on hold.

The Federal Reserve held rates steady on Tuesday at the last meeting of its policy-makers this year, apparently convinced that growth was tame enough to contain inflation. The central bank's policy-makers next meet early in February.

If the economy starts growing much faster than its presumed long-term cruising speed of roughly 2.25 percent and inflation picks up, the Fed is likely to raise rates. Growth much slower than that would make a rate cut more likely.
Two inflation measures in the GDP report pointed to controlled price increases, with scant revisions in each.

The implicit price deflator rose at a revised 1.7 percent rate in the quarter instead of 1.6 percent, compared with 1.8 percent in the second quarter. The fixed-weights measure of price changes rose 2 percent, vs. the previous 1.9 percent estimate and 2.2 percent in the second quarter.
